title: THEY INVITED YOU TO THEIR WEDDING… BUT YOUR CONSCIENCE WON’T LET YOU SAY YES.
paragraphs: THEY INVITED YOU TO THEIR WEDDING… BUT YOUR CONSCIENCE WON’T LET YOU SAY YES.

When someone you love asks you to celebrate something you believe God forbids, what does faithfulness to Jesus actually look like? The answer may break your heart, challenge your convictions, and reveal whether you have learned to speak the truth without forgetting how to love.
The invitation was beautiful.
Your name was written on it. The date was circled. Two people were preparing for one of the most important days of their lives.
And they wanted you there.
Maybe it came from your daughter. Your son. Your brother. Your sister. Your closest friend. Someone you watched grow up. Someone you prayed for when nobody else knew they were struggling.
You should have been smiling.
Instead, you sat there staring at the invitation, feeling something tighten inside your chest.
Because you love them.
You genuinely love them.
But you believe the wedding they are asking you to attend conflicts with what Scripture teaches.
And now a question you never wanted to face is standing in your living room.
If I attend, am I compromising my faith? But if I refuse, am I turning my back on someone Jesus commands me to love?
You can almost hear the arguments already.
“Jesus ate with sinners. Why can't you attend?”
“If you really loved me, you would be there.”
“God knows your heart.”
“Don't be judgmental.”
And perhaps, from the other side:
“If you go, you're approving of sin.”
“Real Christians would never attend.”
“Taking a stand means staying away.”
Everyone seems certain.
But you're the one who has to look into the eyes of someone you love.
You're the one who may have to explain your decision at the family table.
You're the one who may spend the night wondering whether you honored Jesus or wounded someone unnecessarily.
And underneath all the arguments, there is a quieter question.
Lord, how do I remain faithful to Your Word without becoming cruel to someone You created in Your image?
That is where this conversation must begin.
Not with outrage.
Not with fear of what other Christians will say.
Not with the desire to win an argument.
But at the feet of Jesus Christ.
Because this is not merely about whether you should sit in a church pew, stand in a garden, or attend a reception.
It is about what happens when biblical conviction and human relationships collide.
And the way you handle that collision may reveal more about your discipleship than the decision itself.
There is a moment in the Gospel of John that Christians often remember for the wrong reason.
A woman was dragged before Jesus, publicly exposed and accused of adultery.
Her accusers were not interested in restoring her. They wanted a verdict. They wanted condemnation. They wanted to use her shame as a weapon.
Jesus refused to participate in their cruelty.
But He did not declare adultery righteous either.
After her accusers departed, Jesus said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Notice the extraordinary tension.
Mercy without moral surrender.
Truth without public humiliation.
Grace without permission to continue in sin.
Jesus did not choose between compassion and holiness.
He embodied both.
That matters deeply when we talk about weddings that conflict with Christian convictions.
Because some believers think faithfulness requires becoming harsh, while others think love requires surrendering every moral distinction.
But neither response fully reflects Christ.
John 1:14 describes Jesus as “full of grace and truth.”
In Greek, the expression is πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (plērēs charitos kai alētheias).
Grace and truth.
Not grace instead of truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And if we claim to follow Jesus, we cannot treat either as disposable.
Before going further, we must clarify something essential.
Not every wedding that makes a Christian uncomfortable is necessarily contrary to Scripture.
Sometimes what we call conviction is actually family pressure, cultural prejudice, denominational tradition, personal disappointment, or fear of public criticism.
A marriage between people of different ethnic backgrounds is not forbidden by Scripture merely because their cultures differ.
A wedding without the expensive traditions your family expects is not automatically sinful.
A marriage that disappoints your personal preferences is not necessarily a marriage God condemns.
And a Christian must be especially careful not to confuse inherited prejudice with biblical holiness.
But there are situations in which serious theological concerns genuinely arise.

A believer may be invited to a same-sex wedding while holding the historic Christian understanding that marriage is a covenant between one man and one woman, grounded in Genesis 2:24 and reaffirmed by Jesus in Matthew 19:4–6.
Another may be invited to celebrate a relationship that began through adultery, with unresolved questions about an existing marriage covenant.
Someone else may be asked to participate in religious rituals that directly contradict their worship of the one true God.

And another believer may be troubled by a marriage involving a professing Christian and an unbeliever, particularly in light of 1 Corinthians 7:39 and 2 Corinthians 6:14, while recognizing that Christians differ over the application of the latter passage to marriage.
These situations are not identical.
Their biblical considerations are not identical.
And they should not be treated as though one simplistic answer settles every case.
But the deeper question remains.
What does your presence actually communicate?
Because attending a wedding is not exactly the same as having dinner with someone.
A wedding is a public ceremony in which a relationship is formally recognized and celebrated.
Guests are generally invited not merely to observe two people standing together, but to share in their joy and support their union.
For some Christians, that public meaning creates a serious problem when they believe the union itself contradicts God's design.
They ask, “Can I sincerely celebrate what I believe Scripture forbids?”
That is not an unreasonable question.
But another question deserves equal attention.
“Does my physical presence necessarily mean I agree with every moral or theological dimension of the ceremony?”
Not necessarily.
People attend weddings for different reasons, and the meaning of attendance can depend on the ceremony, the role requested, the relationships involved, and the understanding between those present.
A guest is not automatically the officiant.
Sitting in the audience is not identical to making vows.
Attending a reception is not necessarily equivalent to participating in a religious ritual.
And offering kindness to people is not automatically endorsing everything they believe or practice.
The Bible does not contain a verse that explicitly answers every modern wedding-attendance scenario.
That means we must not pretend Scripture speaks more specifically than it does.
We must instead apply its teachings carefully, humbly, and honestly.
And this is where many conversations become uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the strongest biblical conviction is not expressed by making the loudest declaration.
Sometimes it is expressed by refusing to make a decision until you have examined your own heart.
Paul writes in Romans 12:9:
The Greek word translated “without dissimulation” is ἀνυπόκριτος (anypokritos), meaning sincere or unhypocritical.
Christian love must not be a performance.
But neither should Christian holiness.
You can refuse to attend a wedding for the wrong reasons.
You can also attend for the wrong reasons.
You might stay away because you genuinely believe participation would violate your obedience to Christ.
Or you might stay away because you are embarrassed to be associated with someone.
You might attend because you believe you can remain present without affirming what you consider wrong.
Or you might attend because you are terrified of losing approval.
The outward action alone does not tell the whole story.
God sees the heart.
And that should humble all of us.
Remember how Jesus interacted with people whose lives were morally complicated.
In Luke 19, He entered the home of Zacchaeus, a tax collector whose life had been marked by wrongdoing.
People complained that Jesus had become the guest of a sinner.
Yet Christ's presence was not approval of Zacchaeus's exploitation.
It became the setting for repentance and restoration.
Zacchaeus responded by committing to give generously and repay those he had defrauded.
Jesus declared that salvation had come to his house.
That story teaches something precious.
Being present with someone is not always the same as approving their actions.
But we must handle the passage faithfully.
Jesus dining with Zacchaeus does not automatically establish that Christians should attend every ceremony celebrating a relationship they consider sinful.
A meal and a wedding have different purposes.
We cannot simply erase that distinction because it makes our argument easier.
Likewise, Jesus refusing to condemn the woman caught in adultery does not mean He endorsed adultery.
He explicitly called her away from sin.
The Gospel does not permit us to use Jesus as an excuse for either loveless judgment or moral indifference.
We must allow Him to challenge both.
Now consider another passage.
Romans 14 addresses disagreements among believers about disputable practices, including food and the observance of certain days.
Paul writes:
Later, he says:
“Whatsoever is not of faith is sin.” — Romans 14:23, KJV
In its immediate context, Paul is warning believers against acting contrary to their conscience in matters where they are uncertain before God.
The principle is serious.
Do not deliberately violate your conscience.
But conscience must also be instructed by Scripture.
Your conscience is not an infallible voice from heaven.
It can be misinformed.
It can be overly sensitive.
It can be shaped by fear.
It can even become hardened.
That is why the Christian response is not simply, “Whatever feels right must be right.”
It is, “Lord, teach my conscience to agree with Your truth.”
Romans 14 also does not turn clear biblical moral teachings into matters of personal preference.
Its original discussion concerns disputable practices among believers.
Applying its conscience principle to wedding attendance requires careful reasoning rather than assuming the passage directly resolves the moral status of every union.
And perhaps this is what some of us need to hear.
You do not honor God by forcing yourself to participate in something you sincerely believe would be disobedience.
But you also do not honor God by refusing to examine whether your objection actually comes from His Word.
Faithfulness requires both courage and humility.
Then there is 1 Corinthians 10.
Paul addresses participation in pagan religious settings and warns believers against sharing in idolatrous worship.
He distinguishes between ordinary social interactions and participation in worship that compromises allegiance to Christ.
That distinction matters.
There are occasions when participation communicates religious or moral agreement in a way that ordinary friendship does not.
A Christian may therefore have legitimate reasons to decline a particular ceremonial role, prayer, blessing, or ritual.
But again, we must be careful.
Paul was addressing idolatrous worship, not writing a comprehensive guide to modern wedding etiquette.
The passage provides principles about worship, participation, and allegiance. It does not establish that every controversial wedding is equivalent to an idol feast.
Responsible biblical interpretation refuses to claim more than the text supports.
And sometimes, after sincere study, Christians who share a high view of Scripture still reach different conclusions about what attendance communicates in a particular situation.
One believer may decide that attending would publicly affirm something they believe is contrary to Scripture.
Another may conclude that they can attend as an expression of family love while clearly maintaining their theological convictions.
Neither should pretend that the other position is automatically proof of hatred or faithlessness.
The question deserves prayer, discernment, and honest attention to the actual circumstances.
But there is one thing Scripture does not leave uncertain.
Whatever decision you make, you are not permitted to stop loving people.
Jesus says in John 13:35:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.”
And in Matthew 5:44, He commands His followers to love even their enemies.
How much more should we take seriously the dignity of a daughter, a brother, a friend, or a neighbor with whom we disagree?
Disagreement does not cancel human dignity.
Conviction does not excuse cruelty.
And believing someone is wrong does not give you permission to humiliate them.
Imagine a father receiving a wedding invitation from his adult child.
He believes attending would compromise his understanding of biblical marriage.
His child believes refusing to attend means rejection.
There may be tears.
There may be anger.
There may be years of painful history underneath the conversation.
What should the father do?
He should not begin with a public announcement designed to demonstrate how courageous he is.
He should begin with a private conversation.
Perhaps he sits across from his child, struggling to find the words.

“I love you. I need you to know that before anything else. You are my child, and nothing about this conversation changes that. My convictions about marriage come from what I believe Scripture teaches, and I am trying to be faithful to Christ. I understand that my decision may hurt you. I don't want to pretend otherwise. I want to hear how you feel, and I want you to know that I still want a relationship with you.”
That conversation will not necessarily resolve the disagreement.
The child may still feel devastated.
The father may still feel torn.
Love does not guarantee that every boundary will be understood.
And saying something gently does not automatically remove its painful consequences.

But there is a world of difference between a parent who communicates, “I cannot participate in this ceremony because of my convictions,” and one who communicates, “You are no longer worthy of my love.”
One is a disputed moral boundary.
The other is a devastating rejection of a person.
Christians must never confuse the two.
And if you choose not to attend, do not use your absence as a weapon.
Do not organize a campaign to shame the couple.
Do not turn their wedding into an opportunity to embarrass them online.
Do not recruit relatives into a public confrontation.
Do not make their pain a trophy for your religious reputation.
If your conscience leads you to decline, communicate privately and respectfully whenever possible.
Be honest about your convictions without attacking their dignity.
And understand that your decision may have relational costs that cannot be erased by saying you meant well.
You may need to listen to hurt you did not intend.
You may need to remain patient when forgiveness does not come quickly.
You may need to keep showing up in appropriate ways after the ceremony.
A birthday.
A hospital visit.
A difficult season.
A quiet phone call.
A meal when life falls apart.
Because declining one invitation should not become an excuse to abandon a human being.
And if you decide to attend, do not assume your decision requires you to surrender your beliefs.
Be clear in your own conscience about why you are going and what participation you believe is appropriate.
Consider whether you are simply present as a family member or being asked to publicly affirm, bless, officiate, or perform a role that conflicts with your convictions.
Those are meaningful distinctions.
Do not make promises you cannot sincerely make.
Do not participate in religious expressions you believe dishonor Christ.
But do not mistake coldness for courage either.
You can greet people kindly.
You can treat guests with dignity.
You can refuse to make yourself the center of the day.
And you can continue living as a follower of Jesus.
The deeper issue is whether your decision arises from faithful obedience or from the need to prove something about yourself.
Because there is a kind of religious pride that hides behind the language of conviction.
It says, “I am defending God's holiness,” while secretly enjoying the feeling of being morally superior.
It is quick to expose another person's sin but strangely reluctant to confess its own.
It knows how to quote Scripture at someone.
But it has forgotten how to weep.
Jesus told a parable about a Pharisee and a tax collector in Luke 18:9–14.
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other sinners.
The tax collector stood at a distance, unable even to lift his eyes toward heaven.
He cried:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.”
In Greek, Luke 18:13 records:
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
Jesus said it was the tax collector who went home justified rather than the Pharisee.
Not because sin was unimportant.
But because self-righteousness cannot save anyone.
That truth should shake every Christian who is preparing to make a difficult moral decision.
Before you ask whether someone else's relationship honors God, ask whether your own response honors Him.
Before you point to their disobedience, examine your own repentance.
Before you speak about holiness, remember how desperately you need grace.
Because the Gospel is not the story of morally superior people standing above the morally inferior.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
All of us.
The religious.
The rebellious.
The ashamed.
The respectable.
The person who attends.
The person who declines.
The person whose wedding has become the center of controversy.
Every one of us needs the same Savior.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
And Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
This is where the argument becomes personal.
Because you may be right about a biblical principle and still be wrong in the way you treat people.
You may have sound theology and an unrepentant tongue.
You may defend marriage while neglecting your own spouse.
You may condemn sexual immorality while secretly feeding lust.
You may speak passionately about righteousness while refusing to forgive someone who hurt you years ago.
Jesus does not invite us to use another person's life as a distraction from our own need for repentance.
He calls us to follow Him.
Completely.
And that includes the parts of our hearts nobody else sees.
Perhaps the wedding invitation is not the only thing God wants you to examine.
Perhaps He is also confronting your fear of rejection.
Your hunger for approval.
Your resentment toward a family member.
Your habit of confusing harshness with holiness.
Your tendency to remain silent about truth because you desperately want everyone to like you.
Or your tendency to speak truth without compassion because it makes you feel powerful.
Whatever is hidden, bring it to Jesus.
There is no healing in pretending.
There is no freedom in self-righteousness.
And there is no discipleship without surrender.
Now imagine another scene.
The wedding day arrives.
A chair is empty.
Someone notices.
Perhaps the person who declined is at home praying, grieving the distance between conviction and relationship.
Perhaps the couple feels the absence deeply.
Perhaps a guest who chose to attend is sitting quietly, carrying their own questions about what faithfulness requires.
No one in that room knows every motive.
No one sees every prayer.
No one understands every tear.
And that is why we should be cautious about judging one another from a distance.
We can discuss biblical principles.
We can challenge arguments.
We can correct false teaching.
But we are not God.
We do not possess perfect knowledge of every person's conscience, intentions, history, or circumstances.
The same Lord who commands holiness also commands humility.
And there is another danger.
Some Christians become so consumed with whether they should attend a wedding that they forget the people involved will still need love after the wedding is over.
The ceremony lasts hours.
The relationship may last decades.
What will your witness look like five years later?
Will they remember someone who told the truth with tenderness?
Someone who listened?
Someone who maintained convictions without mockery?
Someone who remained willing to help when life became painful?
Or will they remember a Christian who used Scripture as the final sentence in a relationship they no longer wanted to maintain?
You cannot control how another person remembers your decision.
But you can take responsibility for how you behave.
You can apologize for unnecessary harshness without renouncing your convictions.
You can admit when you spoke arrogantly.
You can seek reconciliation where you have caused harm.
You can remain available for honest conversation.
And you can pray for someone without treating them as a project to be fixed.
Because people are not evangelism statistics.
They are human beings.
Made in God's image.
Loved by God in the sense that He calls sinners to repentance and offers salvation through His Son.
And in need of the same grace that rescued us.
Paul writes in Ephesians 4:15 about “speaking the truth in love.”
The Greek expression is ἀληθεύοντες δὲ ἐν ἀγάπῃ (alētheuontes de en agapē).
The verb carries the idea of being truthful or practicing truth, and the surrounding passage concerns believers growing into maturity in Christ.
Truth is not merely a sentence we deliver.
It must characterize how we live.
And love is not merely a feeling we announce.
It must shape how we act.
The goal is not to become people who are always approved by the world.
Nor is it to become people who are proud of being disliked.
The goal is to become more like Jesus.
Jesus was willing to be misunderstood.
He was willing to confront sin.
He was willing to eat with those society rejected.
He was willing to rebuke religious hypocrisy.
He was willing to lose popularity rather than abandon the Father's will.
And He was willing to lay down His life for sinners.
That is the Savior we follow.
Not a Christ invented to excuse every desire.
Not a Christ reshaped into an angry symbol of our cultural battles.
The real Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One who calls us to repentance and offers forgiveness.
The One who never needed to sin in order to love sinners.
The One who never needed to stop loving in order to speak truth.
So should a Christian attend a wedding they believe violates their convictions?
There is no universally applicable yes-or-no answer to every situation.

A Christian should first examine whether the objection is genuinely grounded in Scripture, rather than prejudice or preference. They should consider the nature of the ceremony, what attendance communicates, whether any specific role requires affirmation or participation contrary to conscience, and the likely effects on the people involved.
They should seek wisdom through prayer, careful biblical study, and counsel from mature believers who understand the circumstances.
They should not deliberately act against a conscience they believe is informed by Scripture.
And they should not bind everyone else's conscience with a rule that Scripture itself does not explicitly establish.
Some will conclude they must respectfully decline.
Others will conclude they may attend without surrendering their convictions.
But neither attendance nor absence automatically proves that someone has loved well.
The fruit of that love must be seen in honesty, humility, patience, respect, and faithfulness to Christ.
And regardless of the decision, no Christian is permitted to use it as an excuse for hatred.
This is not moral relativism.
It is an acknowledgment that applying unchanging biblical principles to complex circumstances requires wisdom.
And wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord.
Proverbs 9:10 says:
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.”
Not the fear of social media.
Not the fear of relatives.
Not the fear of being called intolerant.
Not the fear of being called compromising.
The fear of the Lord.
Because one day, the question will not be whether everyone approved of your decision.
It will be whether you sought to honor Christ with a sincere heart.
And perhaps the hardest part of following Jesus is discovering that obedience does not always give you a painless outcome.
Sometimes faithfulness costs you approval.
Sometimes love requires a difficult conversation.
Sometimes refusing to compromise creates distance.
Sometimes remaining present invites criticism.
And sometimes, despite your best efforts, someone you love will misunderstand you.
But the cross reminds us that the right path is not always the comfortable one.
Jesus did not purchase our redemption through popularity.
He gave Himself in sacrificial love.
And He calls His disciples to take up their cross and follow Him.
Not to glorify suffering for its own sake.
Not to manufacture conflict.
But to place allegiance to Christ above the need for human applause.
If your decision is difficult, do not mistake the difficulty for proof that God has abandoned you.
Ask Him for wisdom.
James 1:5 promises that God gives wisdom generously to those who ask in faith.
Pray before you answer the invitation.
Pray before you speak to your family.
Pray before you post your opinion.
And if you have already made a decision you now regret, remember this:
Your story is not beyond the reach of grace.
Perhaps you attended and later became convinced you had compromised your conscience.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Perhaps you refused and later realized you had acted with cruelty or pride.
Seek forgiveness.
Perhaps you handled everything as carefully as you knew how, and the relationship is still fractured.
Continue to entrust what you cannot control to God.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem what sin, pride, fear, and brokenness have damaged.
That does not guarantee every relationship will be restored exactly as you hope.
It does mean your failures do not have to be the final word over your life.
This is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because truth changes with public opinion.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because Jesus Christ entered a fallen world to save sinners and transform lives.
He did not come merely to improve our public image.
He came to reconcile us to God.
And the transformation He brings reaches into our relationships, our decisions, our speech, our convictions, and even our most painful family conflicts.
That is why this message matters beyond one wedding invitation.
Somewhere, a mother is wondering whether her child will ever speak to her again.
Somewhere, a young adult is wondering whether their family still loves them.
Somewhere, a believer is terrified of disappointing their church.
Somewhere, a Christian is struggling to distinguish biblical conviction from inherited fear.
And somewhere, a person who has been wounded by religious harshness is wondering whether Jesus Himself is anything like the people who claim to represent Him.
They need more than slogans.
They need Scripture handled faithfully.
They need conversations marked by humility.
They need believers who can disagree without dehumanizing.
And above all, they need to encounter the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
You may reach someone whose painful question has never been spoken aloud.
The Gospel is too important to be reduced to arguments that win attention while losing sight of souls.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Giving should come from a willing heart.
Not guilt.
Not spiritual pressure.
Not the fear that God will love you less if you cannot afford to contribute.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
And the grace of Jesus Christ is never for sale.

But if this ministry has helped you grow in biblical understanding, confront sin, find encouragement, or return your attention to Christ, your voluntary support can help make these resources available to others.
That benefit is simply a thank-you. It is not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
The greater purpose is to keep directing attention to Jesus, making discipleship resources available, and encouraging believers to remain rooted in the Word of God.
No one should feel that their ability to pay determines their place in the Christian community.
Before you leave, I want to ask you something more important than whether you agree with every conclusion in this article.
When you think about the person whose wedding troubles your conscience, what do you feel?
Anger?
Fear?
Grief?
Confusion?
Love?
Perhaps a mixture of all of them.
Now ask yourself one more question.
If that person were standing in front of me today, would my words and actions help them understand both the holiness of God and the mercy of Jesus Christ?
Not whether they would necessarily agree with you.
Not whether they would immediately repent.
Not whether your relationship would suddenly become easy.
But whether you would be bearing faithful witness to the character of the Savior you proclaim.
That question is worth sitting with.

And if you have walked through a painful disagreement while seeking to remain faithful to Jesus, consider sharing what God taught you. Your testimony may help another believer choose humility over pride and faithfulness over fear.
Most importantly, remember that the purpose of Christian conviction is not to make us feel superior.
It is to lead us into obedience to the One who loved us and gave Himself for us.
We do not follow Jesus merely when His teachings are popular.
We do not abandon His commands when they become uncomfortable.
And we do not discard His command to love when people disagree with us.
We follow Him in truth.
We follow Him in grace.
We follow Him when relationships are complicated and answers are painful.
Because our ultimate allegiance is not to public approval, family pressure, cultural expectation, or even our own reputation.
Our allegiance belongs to Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance.
The same Jesus who offers forgiveness through His blood.
The same Jesus who rose from the grave.
The same Jesus who is able to make all things new.
So whether you attend or decline, do not let the invitation become the end of your love, the excuse for your pride, or the substitute for your obedience.
Let Christ govern your conscience.
Let Scripture shape your convictions.
Let humility temper your words.
Let love guide your conduct.
And let the Gospel remain greater than the controversy.
Because when the flowers have faded, the music has stopped, the photographs have been stored away, and the arguments have grown quiet, something far more important than your reputation will remain.
The witness of how you treated another human being in the name of Jesus.
One day, they may forget the words you used to defend your convictions—but they may never forget whether they could still see the love of Christ in your eyes.
